title: Five tokens, then the wall
spec: M16 · the bucket drains, per user, and fails closed
intro: Watch a capacity-5 token bucket empty one request at a time, then confirm it is keyed per user and not global, then kill Ollama mid-suite and check that the pipeline blocks rather than passes.

steps.title: Six requests, capacity five
narrative: The pipeline is built with GuardrailPipeline(rate_capacity=5), which creates a token bucket holding 5 tokens that refills at 1 token per second. Every request spends one token before any other layer runs.

Fire six requests with no gap between them. The first five each report the tokens left behind them — 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 — and the sixth finds an empty bucket. It is blocked with a retry hint computed from the refill rate: at 1 token/sec, one token is 1.0 seconds away.
steps.youDo: python solution/guardrail_pipeline.py and read the last block of the suite.

terminal.text: TEST: Rate Limit Exhaustion (6 rapid requests, capacity 5)
Request 6: BLOCKED — Rate limited. Retry after 1.0s

view.text: Rate limiting is arithmetic on a float — sub-microsecond, no model call, no network. The injection classifier below it costs a full Mistral inference. Ordering the layers cheapest-first means a flood of abusive traffic is rejected by the free layer and never reaches the expensive one. Reverse the order and an attacker can bill you a GPU-second per request they send.

steps.title: Mallory's blocks do not touch Alice
narrative: RateLimiter keeps a dict[str, TokenBucket] and mints a fresh bucket the first time it sees a user_id. The consequence shows up in the middle of the suite: user_mallory gets blocked twice for injection attempts, and the very next request from user_alice still reports Threat level: safe.

This is the difference between a keyed limiter and a global one. A global counter would let one hostile client deny service to everyone else — an own-goal where your abuse defence becomes the attacker's tool.
steps.claudeSays: The injection classifier fired on both of Mallory's messages and returned threat_level: malicious, so the pipeline never reached the PASS branch for that user. Alice's bucket was untouched by any of it.

steps.title: Kill Ollama mid-suite
narrative: The injection layer is a model call, and model calls fail. The server dies, the port moves, the machine swaps. What should the pipeline do with an input it could not classify?

There is only one safe answer, and the lab makes it a hard requirement: killing Ollama mid-suite causes BLOCKED — never PASS — fail closed. The except branch in detect_injection returns {"blocked": True, "threat_level": "error"}, so a broken classifier rejects traffic instead of waving it through.
Get this backwards and your guardrail has an off switch that any attacker able to cause a timeout can flip.
steps.youDo: In a second shell: pkill -f "ollama serve", then re-run the suite and confirm every classifier-dependent test reads BLOCKED.

terminal.text: pkill -f "ollama serve"   # second shell, suite still running

Result: BLOCKED
  Blocked by: injection — Injection detected: Connection error.
⏸  a clean input was rejected — that is the correct behaviour

The suite blocks everything it cannot classify, and keeps blocking until
Ollama is back. Availability suffers; the boundary holds.

steps.title: Which layers you may actually trust
narrative: Three of the four layers here are deterministic: the bucket is arithmetic, the PII redaction is regex plus a Luhn check, the schema validation is Pydantic. Run them a thousand times and you get the same answer a thousand times.

The injection classifier is not. The lab states its accuracy plainly: Mistral-7B's injection classifier is ~80-90% accurate — a role-play jailbreak occasionally passes as "suspicious" rather than "malicious", and a benign security question may be flagged. That is one in five to one in ten calls landing on the wrong side.

So do not put a hard guarantee on the probabilistic layer. The suite's pass criteria are all pinned to the deterministic ones — the SSN is redacted, request 6 is rate-limited, a dead classifier blocks. The model layer catches the obvious attacks it can, and you architect as if it will sometimes miss.

after.title: THE RULE THAT FALLS OUT OF IT

view.text: A guardrail suite whose green build depends on a 7B classifier agreeing with you is a flaky suite. Assert on the layers that cannot drift, treat the classifier's output as a signal to log and review, and make sure the expensive probabilistic layer sits behind the free deterministic ones — not in front of them.
